name: API Design
description: REST semantics, status codes, versioning, pagination, GraphQL, gRPC and auth flows.

modules.name: The Big Picture
modules.description: What API Design is, what it is for, and the words everything else builds on.

cards.prompt: What is an API?
cards.answer: An Application Programming Interface: a defined way for one piece of software to use another — the operations it offers, the inputs they take and the outputs they return — without knowing how it works inside.
cards.explanation: A library's public functions are an API; so is a web service you call over HTTP. When people say "the API" in web development they usually mean a web API returning JSON.

cards.prompt: What is a REST API, in plain terms?
cards.answer: A web API organised around resources identified by URLs (`/users/42`), manipulated with standard HTTP methods (`GET` to read, `POST` to create, `PUT`/`PATCH` to update, `DELETE` to remove), usually exchanging JSON.
cards.explanation: REST reuses the web's existing machinery — URLs, methods, status codes, caching — so any HTTP client can use it. It is the most common style for public web APIs.

cards.prompt: What do the HTTP status code classes mean?
cards.answer: 1xx informational, 2xx success (`200 OK`, `201 Created`), 3xx redirection (`301`, `304`), 4xx client error — the request was wrong (`400`, `401`, `403`, `404`), 5xx server error — the server failed (`500`, `503`).
cards.explanation: Returning the right class matters: clients retry 5xx errors but should not retry a 4xx without changing the request. Returning `200` with an error message in the body breaks every generic client and monitor.

cards.prompt: What are an endpoint, a request and a response in a web API?
cards.answer: An endpoint is a URL plus method the API accepts, such as `GET /orders/7`. The request is what the client sends (method, path, headers, optional body); the response is what comes back (status code, headers, body).
cards.explanation: API documentation is essentially a list of endpoints with the requests they accept and responses they return. OpenAPI is the standard machine-readable format for writing that down.

cards.prompt: How do clients usually prove who they are to an API?
cards.answer: By sending a credential with each request, usually in the `Authorization` header: an API key for server-to-server calls, or an access token (often a JWT obtained through OAuth) on behalf of a user.
cards.explanation: Credentials must only ever travel over HTTPS and should never be committed to source code. Authentication answers "who are you?"; authorisation answers "what may you do?".

modules.name: REST & HTTP Semantics
modules.description: Methods, status codes, idempotency and the conventions clients actually rely on.

cards.prompt: Which HTTP methods are safe, and which are idempotent?
cards.answer: Safe (no side effects): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent (repeating gives the same result): GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE. POST and PATCH are neither by default.
cards.explanation: This is not pedantry — proxies, browsers and retry libraries act on it. A GET that mutates will be triggered by a prefetcher. A non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key so a client retry after a timeout does not double-charge.

cards.prompt: When do you use 400 vs 401 vs 403 vs 404 vs 409 vs 422 vs 429?
cards.answer: 400 malformed request; 401 not authenticated; 403 authenticated but not allowed; 404 not found (or hiding existence from an unauthorised caller); 409 conflict with current state; 422 syntactically valid but semantically invalid; 429 rate limited.
cards.explanation: 401 versus 403 is the pair most often confused: 401 means 'who are you?', 403 means 'I know who you are and no'. Returning 404 instead of 403 is a deliberate choice to avoid leaking that a resource exists.

cards.prompt: Offset pagination vs cursor pagination
cards.answer: Offset is simple and allows jumping to a page; cursor is stable under concurrent writes and stays fast at depth.

left.title: ?page=500&size=20
points: Easy to implement, arbitrary page jumps
Items shift between pages as data changes
Duplicates and skips under active writes

right.title: ?after=<cursor>
points: Keyset seek — constant time at any depth
No page numbers or total count
Cursor must encode the sort key

cards.explanation: Use cursors for feeds, logs and anything large or live. Encode the cursor opaquely (base64 of sort key plus tiebreaker id) so you can change the underlying scheme without breaking clients.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Paging through results

cards.prompt: You need to change a response field's meaning. How do you avoid breaking every client?
cards.answer: Do not change it. Add a new field, populate both, migrate clients, then remove the old one after a deprecation window — the expand/contract pattern. Reserve version bumps (`/v2`) for changes that cannot be made additively.
cards.explanation: Backwards-compatible changes: adding optional fields, adding endpoints, adding enum values *if clients tolerate unknowns*. Breaking: removing or renaming fields, tightening validation, changing types or semantics. Document which guarantees you offer, or clients will assume all of them.

cards.prompt: What belongs in an API error response?
cards.answer: A stable machine-readable code, a human-readable message, the field(s) at fault for validation errors, and a correlation/trace id. Never a stack trace or internal identifiers.
cards.explanation: RFC 9457 (problem details) standardises this shape. Machine codes let clients branch without string-matching prose; the trace id turns a user's screenshot into a log query. Keep internal detail out — it is reconnaissance for an attacker.

resources.title: RFC 9457 — Problem Details for HTTP APIs

modules.name: Styles & Auth
modules.description: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC, plus the auth flows you will actually implement.

cards.prompt: REST, GraphQL or gRPC — how do you choose?
cards.answer: REST for public, cacheable, resource-shaped APIs. GraphQL when many different clients need different slices of a graph and over-fetching hurts. gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where latency, streaming and typed contracts matter.
cards.explanation: GraphQL moves query complexity to the server: you must add depth limits, cost analysis and dataloaders or you have shipped an N+1 generator with a DoS vector. gRPC needs a proxy for browsers (gRPC-Web) and is harder to debug by hand.

cards.prompt: Which OAuth 2.1 flow should a web or mobile app use, and why?
cards.answer: Authorization code flow with PKCE. The implicit flow is deprecated because it returns tokens in the URL fragment, and password grant is deprecated because it hands your credentials to the client.
cards.explanation: PKCE binds the authorisation code to the client that requested it with a code verifier, so an intercepted code is useless. Public clients (SPAs, mobile) cannot keep a secret, which is exactly why PKCE exists.

resources.title: OAuth 2.0 — Authorization code flow with PKCE

cards.prompt: JWT vs opaque session tokens
cards.answer: JWTs are self-contained and verifiable without a lookup; opaque tokens are meaningless strings resolved against server state.

left.title: JWT
points: Larger; leaks claims if not encrypted

right.title: Opaque session
points: Revoke instantly by deleting the record
Requires a lookup (usually a cache hit)

cards.explanation: The usual compromise: short-lived JWT access tokens (minutes) plus a revocable refresh token. Always pin the algorithm on verification — accepting `alg: none` or letting the token choose HMAC vs RSA is a classic critical bug.

resources.title: RFC 8725 — JSON Web Token Best Current Practices

cards.prompt: How do you rate limit an API, and what should the response tell the client?
cards.answer: Token bucket or sliding window per key (user, IP, API key) in a shared store such as Redis. Return 429 with `Retry-After` and `RateLimit-*` headers so well-behaved clients can back off precisely.
cards.explanation: Token bucket allows bursts while capping the average — usually what you want. Clients should retry with exponential backoff plus jitter; synchronised retries cause the thundering herd that turns a blip into an outage.

resources.title: IETF — RateLimit header fields for HTTP

modules.name: Designing APIs People Can Use
modules.description: Resource naming, filtering, PATCH semantics, long-running operations, webhooks, contracts and deprecation.

cards.prompt: What are the conventions for REST resource URLs?
cards.answer: Plural nouns for collections (`/orders`), an ID for an item (`/orders/42`), nesting only for true containment (`/orders/42/items`), HTTP methods as the verbs, lowercase with hyphens, and query parameters for filtering, sorting and paging (`/orders?status=paid&sort=-created_at`).
cards.explanation: Avoid verbs in paths (`/getOrders`, `/createOrder`); for genuine actions that are not CRUD, a sub-resource (`POST /orders/42/cancellation`) or an action endpoint used consistently is fine. Consistency across the whole API matters more than any individual rule.

cards.prompt: `PUT` vs `PATCH` (JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch)
cards.answer: PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation sent; PATCH applies a partial change. JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) sends a partial document, with `null` meaning delete; JSON Patch (RFC 6902) sends a list of operations (`add`, `remove`, `replace`, `test`).

right.title: PATCH
points: Merge Patch: partial JSON, null deletes

cards.explanation: Merge Patch is simpler and covers most cases, but cannot set a field to null or edit single array elements. JSON Patch is precise and can include `test` for optimistic concurrency. Whichever you choose, document it — "PATCH with a partial body" is ambiguous otherwise.

cards.prompt: Generating a report takes three minutes. How should the API expose it?
cards.answer: Return `202 Accepted` with a `Location` of a status resource (`/reports/jobs/123`). Clients poll it (honouring a `Retry-After`) or receive a webhook; when done it links to the result. Support cancellation with `DELETE` on the job.
cards.explanation: Holding an HTTP request open for minutes fails against load balancer and client timeouts and ties up server resources. Modelling the job as a resource also gives you retries, progress reporting and an audit trail for free.

cards.prompt: What makes a webhook implementation robust and secure?
cards.answer: Sign every payload (HMAC of the body plus a timestamp) and have receivers verify the signature in constant time and reject old timestamps to block replays. Retry with backoff on failure, include an event ID so receivers can deduplicate, and let receivers acknowledge quickly and process asynchronously.
cards.explanation: Delivery is at-least-once and unordered, so receivers must be idempotent and must not assume sequence. Provide a way to replay missed events and to rotate signing secrets without downtime.

cards.prompt: What does an OpenAPI description give you?
cards.answer: A machine-readable contract for an HTTP API — paths, parameters, request and response schemas, auth — from which you can generate documentation, client SDKs, server stubs, mock servers and request validation, and diff versions to detect breaking changes in CI.
cards.explanation: Contract-first (write the spec, then implement) forces design review before code; code-first (generate the spec from annotations) keeps it in sync effortlessly. Either way, lint it and fail the build on unintended breaking changes.

cards.prompt: You must retire `/v1/orders` used by hundreds of external clients. How?
cards.answer: Announce a timeline, mark responses with the `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers plus a link to the migration guide, measure who still calls it (per API key), contact those clients directly, and shut down only after usage has actually dropped — optionally with scheduled brownouts first.
cards.explanation: Usage data beats announcements: most breakage comes from clients nobody knew about. A brownout (returning errors for a short, announced window) flushes out forgotten integrations while there is still time to fix them.

resources.title: RFC 8594 — The Sunset HTTP Header Field

cards.prompt: This resolver makes the query `{ posts(first: 50) { author { name } } }` issue 51 database queries. Why, and what fixes it?
cards.answer: Each post's `author` field resolves independently, so 50 posts trigger 50 author lookups — the N+1 problem inside GraphQL. Batch them with a DataLoader: collect every author ID requested in one tick, fetch them in a single `WHERE id IN (...)` query, and cache per request.
cards.explanation: DataLoader instances must be per-request, never global, or one user's data can be served to another. Pair batching with query depth and cost limits, because clients control query shape.

cards.prompt: How do you evolve a Protocol Buffers message without breaking existing clients?
cards.answer: Never change or reuse a field's number or type — the number is the wire identity. Add new fields with new numbers (old readers skip unknown fields), and when removing a field, mark its number and name `reserved` so nobody reuses them.
cards.explanation: Field names can change freely because they do not appear on the wire, but numbers are forever. In proto3 every field is optional with a zero default, so clients must treat "missing" and "zero" carefully (or use `optional` for presence tracking).

cards.prompt: API keys vs OAuth access tokens
cards.answer: An API key is a long-lived static secret that identifies a calling application; an OAuth access token is short-lived, scoped, issued on behalf of a user or client, and refreshable.

left.title: API key
points: Leaks in client code or repos

cards.explanation: API keys suit server-to-server calls where you control both ends — store them hashed, allow several per account for rotation, scope them, and never embed them in front-end code. Use OAuth when acting on behalf of users or when third parties integrate.
